turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Morning, Dana. Quick heads-up — I spun up the new staging instances for the product API. No autoscaling on them yet, just fixed capacity to keep costs predictable.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Got it. But we've got that big marketing push next week — you sure fixed capacity is enough? Traffic could triple overnight.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I'll monitor it. If it gets hairy, I can scale manually. Honestly, autoscaling adds config overhead and I'd rather not deal with it right now.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Your call. Just don't let it bite us.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: It won't. I've got this.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Sam, what the hell happened? The service went down hard during the spike this morning.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Yeah... I know. The instances maxed out CPU and memory, and the whole thing just fell over. And because the product API is upstream, the cart and checkout services cascaded down with it.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: So the fixed capacity was a bad idea, huh?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Clearly. I've already enabled autoscaling on all the instances — min 2, max 10, with a CPU-based policy. That should absorb any future spikes.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Good. But what about the dependent services? They went down too.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: I'm on it. I'm adding circuit breakers on the dependent calls so if the product API hiccups again, the downstream services fail gracefully instead of crashing. That's the next step.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Alright. And while you're at it — I noticed you deleted the end-to-end tests to save time before the release. That's why the app broke right after we pushed, isn't it?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Yeah, that was a mistake. I've put them back in the pipeline. They'll run on every commit now, no exceptions.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Good. Let's hope the next release stays healthy.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Hey Sam, the release went out last night — app stayed healthy, no incidents. Nice work.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Thanks. But honestly, I need to admit something — I was wrong about the autoscaling fix.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: What do you mean? It handled the spike fine this time.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: It did, but only because the spike was moderate. I ran a load test yesterday with a real peak — autoscaling alone didn't stop the cascading failures. The instances scaled up, but the dependent services still timed out and dragged each other down.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: So autoscaling wasn't enough?

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Turns out that wasn't enough. I've replaced the autoscaling-only approach with circuit breakers as the primary defense. Now, even if the product API gets overwhelmed, the downstream services fail fast and stay up. Autoscaling is still there, but it's secondary.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: That makes sense. So the real fix was the circuit breakers, not just adding more instances.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Exactly. I was wrong to think scaling alone would save us. The circuit breakers are what keep the whole system resilient. And the end-to-end tests are still in the pipeline — that's non-negotiable now.

turns.speaker: Dana
turns.text: Good lesson. Glad we caught it before the real traffic hit.

turns.speaker: Sam
turns.text: Me too. Better to learn it in a load test than in production.
